My friends who know prisons don't watch movies!  But "Shawshank" is cinema storytelling at its finest.  If you love a good story, and can handle some of the rougher things in life, this is your movie.The choice of Morgan Freeman for the narrator, Red, was inspired.  But I'm beginning to wonder if casting Morgan Freeman is ever less than inspired at any time, for any part.  His warm voice and gentle accent is impossible not to listen to.  I think that voice could keep your attention reading the dictionary aloud.  His face is always interesting.  If Morgan Freeman is in a movie, I'm willing to give the movie a chance.This is the second Tim Robbins movie I ever saw.  And this is quite a departure from his "Nuke" LaLouche in "Bull Durham".  His performance is intelligent, understated, intense.  He is a great movie actor--he doesn't need to speak to communicate volumes.But the real star of "Shawshank" is Stephen King.  He has become the premier storyteller of our day.  He puts words together to make magic like no one I've ever read.  And his stories translate so well to the screen.  "Stand By Me" proved it.   "Shawshank" confirms it.  All hail, Stephen King!If you haven't seen "The Shawshank Redemption", do so.  Maybe, like me, you'll be looking to buy the video for your small collection of movies to be seen over and over again.

review: Robbins and Freeman excellent with magnificent supporting cast

I'm not one for physical violence, but in this film the violence is limited and justified by the story line, as this is inevitable in prisons at any moment. But the film is much more  friendship and love, with its humourous moments.Photographed almost in a 50s style but with an obviously 90s mentality, Roger Deakins not only fills the screen visually but also emotionally, an extraordinary feat indeed. Thomas Newman caught that emotion well and his accompanying music is very correct. Morgan Freeman pleases me more and more each time I see him, though I still feel that it is in `Driving Miss Daisy' where he gives his best performance. He has wisely kept out of Sidney Poitier stereotyping, though it must be said that times have changed and Poitier had to reflect social conditions of his time and thus opened the way for excellent actors like Freeman and Denzel Washington. Frank Darabont has created a wonderful film  but number two best of all time in the IMDb scale? Well, I can give it a high 8 out of ten, about the same as the other Darabont/Stephen King film `The Green Mile', another prison film, hard, harsh. You might like to try Susan Sarandon and Sean Penn in Tim Robbins' film `Dead Man Walking' (also filmed by Roger Deakins) which has a similarly powerful message, but without so much violence.

review: "Get bust living - or get busy dying"
main_review: 'The Shawshank Redemption' is based heavily upon Stephen King's short story 'Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption' - adapted for screen by Writer/Director Frank Darabont (screenwriter for 'The Fly II' and 'Indiana Jones 4.') Since this film has graced the silver screen, Darabont has also adapted King's 'The Green Mile' and 'The Majestic' with great success. This has truly sparked off a trend of King adaptations such as 'Night Flier,' 'Hearts in Atlantis' and 'Dream Catcher.' In this film an innocent man is wrongly accused of the murder of his wife and her lover, and imprisoned in 'Shawshank Prison' for two life-terms. Within the prison walls (some stronger than others) the enigma unravels as 'Andy Dufresne' (Tim Robbins - 'Arlington Road') meets extraordinary people with the gift of 'seeing hope through the bars,' such as 'Red' (Morgan Freeman - 'Dreamcatcher') who tells Andy to "Get bust living - or get busy dying." Under the harsh conditions in which Andy's love for reading, music and friendship are exploited (sentencing him to the light-devoid 'hole') he uses all his skill and logic to conduct a plan unlike any other - escape and exploit 'Warden Norton' (Bob Gunton - 'Patch Adams') and start living again.This film is successful due to the simplistic (yet ideal) cinematography, the splendid acting, the real emotion and the fact that Darabont employs many of the same cast his other films ('The Green Mile' and 'The Majestic') - generating a wonderful, intimate atmosphere between the cast. This film seems like a much-loved, family project - rather than a faceless Hollywood production...

I came expecting a masterpiece and left with the impression I'd seen a relatively unremarkable film with pretensions of profundity. Put plainly, the primary message is "Hope sustains the human spirit in a world of hardship and despair," which is a truism that would fit nicely in a fortune cookie. Nonetheless, the power of hope can serve as an affecting theme. Perhaps this common theme is taken by so many as great depth because so much of Hollywood's product these days is appallingly shallow or callously brutal. Apparently, the public is desperate for something to care about.The direction is somewhat mannered and reminiscent of older films, which in itself is neither good nor bad. But in this case it blends with a storyline that seems virtually comprised of movie cliches of prison life. The characters are also stereotypes: the evil warden (bible-toting, naturally!), the brutal and inhuman prison guard, the gang of prison buddies, the gang of cell block victimizers, the experienced convict who has mastered the system (played by Morgan Freeman), the enigmatic newcomer who works subtly to subvert the system (played by Tim Robbins) -- all the classics on parade, with few of the unnecessary peculiarities that define real human beings! We've seen them all before, and in more realistic guise. These one-dimensional characters function with the monomania of gears in a machine, churning out a largely predictable plot. This is typical of allegorical stories, and I suspect this story can be read as allegory (which is not surprising, since it is based on a Stephen King tale). Regardless, I can honestly say not one element of the plot caught me by surprise.
In all, the film seems to hover in tone and content somewhere between reality and the idealized world of the fable (say, a fable like The Green Mile, a movie by the same director). Many of the story elements seemed in one way or another contrived, which left me feeling vaguely dissatisfied and manipulated. Even good devices -- such as the well-known tendency of prisoners to become programmed by prison life, resulting in problems when they return to society (a syndrome referred to in the film as becoming "institutionalized") -- lose some of their power through a rather heavy-handed treatment. However, the climax of the story (although predictable) was very well-constructed and quite effective.Regarding the acting, Tim Robbins is fair, but hardly awe-inspiring. On the other hand, Morgan Freeman, one of my favorite actors, is a rare talent who is almost certain to turn in a superb performance. This movie is no exception, and I believe if viewers think about it, they will realize that the strongest, most eloquent and moving portion of the movie is the last half hour in which his character, Red, is the focus of attention. The extended denouement almost saved the film for me, but for this viewer the movie reached its end with only a hint of the title's promised redemption.For those of you who want to see a prison movie that is deeper, more profound, has better dialogue, plotting, and symbolism; and presents characters in now familiar roles (your assignment, compare and contrast!) but with considerably more substance and reality, check out Cool Hand Luke. It may not spell out what it's all supposed to mean in Shawshank's user-friendly, large-print narration, but it is nonetheless in all respects the superior movie.

review: NOT THAT GREAT!!! OPEN YOUR FRIGGIN EYES!!!!!!
main_review: Many, many people jock this movie, calling it an intelligent, philosophical and moving epic, but It's really not all that. It is a good movie, but it is not great or thought provoking at all. That year, 1994, was a great year for movies considering Pulp Fiction, Ed Wood and Quiz Show among others, yet people think Forrest Gump and Shawshank Redemption are great' movies? Gag me.Here's some of the problems (Don't read this if you haven't seen the movie)Morgan Freeman's character - Don't get me wrong Freeman is a great actor (even if he always plays the same part) but seriously, did you ever watch MTV's Scared Straight' or listened to Chris Rock's stand-up? Now tell me what kind of 18-year-old murderer goes to prison and kicks around using words that would make Edgar Allen Poe go get his copy of Webster's? Freeman's character's narration also served as a purpose to constantly bludgeon the viewer with 2nd rate philosophy people who've never been to prison come up with. By the end I was literally exhausted from the constant stream of corny insight I've already heard. Tell the truth now... If you saw a murderer on the evening news you'd probably want him dead or at least in prison for life, yet here you're supposed to rejoice in his parole as a result of a tired, bitch-em-out-I-don't-care speech that only seems to come up in movies. Another detraction to the narration is Morgan Freeman dropping the F, it never sounds right.The Warden - How many absolutely despicable characters has that guy played? Has anyone that evil ever run a prison? That is classic jail movie material. Obviously the filmmakers realize people will be upset about glorifying criminals so the answer is to make the authority pure evil. How irritating If you want to convey criminals, just show them having fun and being real people; don't try to cover it up with evil police, try Bonnie and Clyde or Pulp Fiction, much more interesting.Brooks  Some serious button pushing here. Brooks is a typical, lame attempt to draw out some sentiment. The bird thing is a rip off of Escape from Alcatraz and like Freeman's character he's a great guy who happened to commit an offense so despicable he's in one of the most secure prisons in the country, but we can forget about that, right? The `Brooks was here' hanging himself because he can't keep up is another Hollywood favorite. Who hangs themselves? My gosh, at Nuremberg guys took poison to avoid being hanged because of the shame and disrespect. Yet, Brooks hung himself when at his age he could have waited a week and let nature take its course. Or better yet if Brooks got an old-fashioned whore and binged himself to death on alcohol and mind-altering drugs. Almost sounds like fun, who would prefer hanging? You know who, a character in a movie. That pretty much sums up the Shawshank Redemption, for what its aiming for it misfires because there is nothing genuine or authentic about it.

review: "Put your trust in the Lord  your ass belongs to me"
main_review: So says the warden of Shawshank prison, though Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) finds it belongs to a lot more people in this often-harrowing tale.The Shawshank Redemption is a very, very clever film in that it takes its call from elder cinema, meaning it can net not only acclaim but also a wider audience. It's surely no coincidence that the first sound we hear  before the titles have even begun to roll - is that of The Ink Spots singing "If I Didn't Care". The shot pans out to Tim Robbins in an old-fashioned automobile and then to a courtroom where his last words to his wife were "I'll see you in Hell". No profanity from a bitter man in 90's cinema, though expletives do flavour the piece, with 24 uses of the f-word and 48 minor swearwords.A few minutes into the film and part of the reason is given: the setting is 1947. However, the oldstyle trappings of the piece never leave it: violence and sexual activity are never laboured on. Beatings are delivered in shadow, or, in the case of Andy's first, the camera discretely pulls back and turns a corner while we just hear the sound. Note we are never shown that Andy is raped, we are just told that he is by Morgan Freeman's narration. That's another strong point of the film, and also an historical device, that of first person narration. Freeman adds a constant magnetism to the film; his voice-over a necessity considering it takes place over 20 years. Refreshingly, the ageing process is used subtly, if at all, rather than using unconvincing prosthetics. A little grey to Morgan's hair and the power of persuasion is all that is needed to carry out the illusion of time passing.Another interesting point is that of race. Someone once told me they didn't like the film because they saw the black/white male bonding between Robbins and Freeman as too contrived and worthy. I told them that this showed a suspect attitude on their part as Ellis Redding's skin colour hadn't occurred to me, nor is it ever mentioned throughout the film. It isn't an issue that Redding is black, he just IS. Ultimately, the redemption of the title comes from Robbins' humanitarian intellectualism against the warden's fundamental religious beliefs. But the ultimate testament to erstwhile cinema is that of two things: plot and character. It's this strength of character, not to mention two superb understated leads, which mean you can watch it again and again, even when one viewing reveals the twist in the tale. All the characters are three-dimensional, breathing human beings that get not lines, but emotions and beliefs. Occasionally some  not much, but some  of the dialogue can strain towards the overly sentimental. Perhaps this is what produced the nauseating tagline "Fear can hold you prisoner  hope can set you free". Yuck! But generally this pleasantly paced, well-told tale hits the target in it's own relaxed way. Far from pedestrian, the timing of the film is like that of drinking a cool beer on a hot summer's roof, or a whole yardful of inmates standing stock still to the beauty of Mozart. The Shawshank Redemption was released the same year as Pulp Fiction, yet both of them were disgraced at the Oscars by the forgettable Forrest Gump. A great oversight.

review: The most satisfying ending in Cinema
main_review: I just watched Shawshank for the nth time tonight (it was on TNT), and realized why I enjoyed the movie so much: it had one of the most cinematic, enthralling, and satisfying conclusion in movie history.  Not that I am dismissing the great story, honest and absorbing characters, and memorable scenes (the scene where an entire field full of inmates seemingly hypnotized by Mozart's opera music comes to mind).  The ending where all of the warden's sins were conveniently exposed may sound contrived in other movies, but brilliant writing filled with dry wit carried the scene through marvelously (Red: "I'd like to think the last thing that went through the warden's head - other than the bullet - was how in hell Andy Dufresne got the best of him").  And the way the last scene was put together, where Red's narration of 'hopes' melts into a scene where his hopes comes true (when he actually crossed the border and reunited with his old friend), was just magical.  It makes me glad that my girlfriend pushed me into watching it ("But it's just a stupid prison movie!" I lamented).  How I was wrong!

Perhaps the greatest challenge of the AMPAS is determining what defines a "Best Picture." I have heard it defined from some forgotten source directly tied to the AMPAS that a Best Picture is one that holds itself superb in the following three categories: Direction, Writing, and Acting, not necessarily in that order. A good example would be Citizen Kane, arguably the most worthy winner of these three categories (Kane lost to How Green and never picked up the Best Picture statue). However, it is certain that the greatest film of all time would need to excel especially in one field: Originality. How many people would even go bother to see another interpertation of Titanic? However, if this particular film had come out before the Cameron version, it would certainly be hailed with critical acclaim. Shawshank is one that meets the AMPAS standards of excellence, and most certainly would have taken the Best Picture title, if not for Forrest Gump, a film which many members perhaps found it impossible to not vote for due to the momentum it had gained. If Shawshank had been nominated almost any other year of this decade, the statue would have been a lock. However, we must look at Shawshank not as the year's Best Picture, but as a film in the long timeline of movie history, a film which tells an original story with original acting style and original directing. Can we look at Shawshank and with all sincerity call it the greatest film ever? Before deciding, a prerequisite should be to see at least 50 of the best films of this century. In this way, Shawshank loses the advantage of being fresh in our memory, losing the emotional effect, and must bow to the annals of time as do all the other superb films of history. Shawshank is not the Best Picture of all time nor the greatest film of all time. This is a fact we must face and learn to live with, no matter how much the storyline touched us all.

review: An excellent film with some deep thought provoking meanings

Being convicted of a crime that they did not commit and locked up for life with the very worst types of human beings.  How being institutionalised is the only way to survive, but when it ends there is no way to go, no way to return to a former life. All human existence is based on a survival instinct. Once that is destroyed, death is a welcome relief.The story hinges around three men,  one who never lost it and escaped to live again, one who nearly lost it but re-gained hope from the first and one who lost it and killed himself. Although the setting was the harsh and hostile environment of prison, it could have been any other institution, a hospital, an old peoples home even a family home.Andy Dufresne is different because he never lost the hope of escape, he used the weaknesses of others, the corruption of prison officials, the internal prison system to help his long term plan.  He had the great advantage over the others, including the Prison staff of being , intellignet knowledgable and clever. Such people always win through.  I did not know what the end was going to be, a clever piece of filming.  Although the meassage was not lost,It should give encouragement to all those who find themselves in a similar position. The justice system, although far from perfect is much improved so miscarriages can now be corrected. But I still wounder what it must feel like to be in the situation of Andy Dufresne but without his abilities.Let's have more such films that provoke the senses and emotions as this one did.  I make no excuse in adding to the hundreds of comments already make on this film , although I have not read them because I wanted mine to be original. But no doubt other thinking people would have made similar comments.  I hope that writers, producers and sponsors read these comments and take note when making more such films

review: A Timeless Masterpiece: The Shawshank Redemption
main_review: The Shawshank Redemption stands as a quintessential example of cinematic brilliance, weaving a tale of hope, friendship, and resilience that transcends time. Directed by Frank Darabont and based on a novella by Stephen King, this film has rightfully earned its place as one of the greatest movies ever made.From its opening scenes, The Shawshank Redemption captivates with its powerful storytelling and complex characters. Tim Robbins delivers a masterful performance as Andy Dufresne, a banker wrongfully imprisoned for the murder of his wife and her lover. Robbins' portrayal of Dufresne's quiet dignity and unyielding hope anchors the film, making his journey from despair to redemption deeply compelling.Morgan Freeman's portrayal of Ellis "Red" Redding is nothing short of extraordinary. Freeman's nuanced and heartfelt performance provides the perfect counterbalance to Robbins' Andy, and his narration adds a layer of profound wisdom and introspection. The chemistry between Robbins and Freeman is palpable, elevating their characters' friendship to one of the most memorable relationships in film history.The film's direction, by Frank Darabont, is meticulous and immersive. The storytelling is rich with emotional depth, and Darabont's attention to detail in every frame ensures that the film resonates long after the credits roll. The cinematography, with its evocative use of light and shadow, further enhances the mood and atmosphere, capturing both the bleakness of Shawshank Prison and the glimmers of hope within.Thomas Newman's score complements the film's themes perfectly, with a hauntingly beautiful soundtrack that underscores the emotional weight of the story. The music subtly weaves through the narrative, enhancing the impact of each pivotal moment and contributing to the film's timeless quality.

The Shawshank Redemption is a cinematic masterpiece that transcends time and genre. It's a story of resilience, friendship, and the unwavering human spirit. Tim Robbins delivers a powerful performance as Andy Dufresne, a banker unjustly sentenced to life imprisonment. Morgan Freeman's portrayal of Red, a seasoned inmate, is equally captivating. Their bond forms the heart of the film, a testament to the enduring power of human connection.The film's exploration of themes like hope, redemption, and the corrupting influence of power is both thought-provoking and emotionally resonant. The stunning cinematography and haunting score further enhance the film's impact. The Shawshank Redemption is a must-watch for anyone seeking a truly inspiring and unforgettable cinematic experience.

The Shawshank Redemption is a timeless masterpiece that transcends the traditional confines of the prison drama genre, offering a profound exploration of hope, friendship, and the human spirit. Directed by Frank Darabont and based on Stephen King's novella, this 1994 film has rightfully earned its place as one of the greatest films of all time.At its core, The Shawshank Redemption is a story about hope in the face of despair. The film follows Andy Dufresne (played by Tim Robbins), a banker wrongfully convicted of murder, as he navigates the harsh realities of life inside Shawshank Prison. Despite the brutal and oppressive environment, Andy maintains a quiet dignity and resilience, which ultimately inspires those around him, including his friend Red (played by Morgan Freeman).Robbins delivers a career-defining performance as Andy, capturing the character's internal strength and unwavering optimism with subtlety and grace. Morgan Freeman's portrayal of Red is equally compelling, bringing warmth and wisdom to the role of a man who has become institutionalized by decades of incarceration. Freeman's narration adds a layer of depth to the story, guiding the audience through the emotional highs and lows of prison life with his iconic voice.The film's cinematography, by Roger Deakins, is visually stunning, with Shawshank Prison itself almost becoming a character in the story. The bleak, gray walls of the prison contrast sharply with the rare moments of beauty and freedom, such as the memorable scene where Andy plays Mozart over the prison's loudspeakers, momentarily lifting the spirits of every inmate.Thomas Newman's hauntingly beautiful score further enhances the film's emotional impact, perfectly complementing the narrative's themes of redemption and hope. The music swells at just the right moments, evoking a sense of yearning and transcendence that stays with the viewer long after the credits roll.What makes The Shawshank Redemption truly extraordinary is its exploration of the human spirit. The film delves into the complexities of life behind bars, showing how hope and friendship can survive even in the darkest of places. Andy's relentless pursuit of freedom, both physical and spiritual, serves as a powerful reminder that the human spirit can endure and overcome even the most daunting of circumstances.The Shawshank Redemption is more than just a prison drama; it is a meditation on the power of hope and the resilience of the human soul. main_review: Shawshank Redemption is my favorite film of all. In my eyes, it's the G. O. A. T that I judge every other movie by the standards of. You might expect a 10, but I don't give 10s for anything. A 9.5 is the highest score attainable on my scale, and to date, I have only given that to 9 films out of 1,587 films I have watched (might be a few missing that I watched in my childhood I don't remember). I won't go deep into the plot. Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), a shrewd banker, is convicted for the murders of his wife and her lover even after claiming innocence. They send him to a fictional Shawshank State Prison to serve two lifetimes without parole. At Shawshank, he befriends Red Redding (Morgan Freeman), who is also in prison for murder decades earlier and a master smuggler. While claiming his innocence through it all, Andy has to watch his days pass through troubling and painful obstacles to the end of his days as the film credits run. I'm kidding, of course! Actually, no, not this Andy. This Andy struggles and triumphs.This film inspires me each time I watch, and the ending leaves tears, no matter how many times I have seen it already (fourth for me). More than anything, this is a story of hope. I believe hope is perhaps the most important emotion that a person can have. Red thinks hope is a dangerous thing, but Andy replies, "hope is a good thing, maybe the best of things, and no good thing ever dies." Andy does just that, holds onto hope through the worst of things. One has a simple choice in life, as Andy says. Get busy living, or get busy dying. You must choose hope and living every time, no matter the odds or the will required to overcome the mightiest of obstacles. Whether it's a physical prison or a metaphorical prison, hope is your salvation. This film is the epitome of just that. It's also about the power of friendship, freedom, and the triumph of the human spirit.I don't think anyone can make this film better. The filmmakers did justice, and then some, to Stephen King's original novella. It is one of my favorite literatures of all-time, but the film is even better. The technicals are close to perfect. Script, directing, acting, editing, cinematography, and music. The brilliant cinematography and masterful dialogue keep you captivated in every scene. Robbins and Freeman are sensational in every scene and tailormade for their respective roles. The entire cast is great in their respective roles.Some tidbits that I found interesting. Robbins went into solitary confinement to prepare for his role. This film received 7 Oscar nominations but didn't win any in a historic snub (Step aside, Forrest Gump and Pulp Fiction!). It was also a flop at the theater, losing money. It became the most rented film of 1995 and made millions as a rental/sales. The filmmakers sent King a $5,000 check for the story rights, but King framed it and sent it back to the director, Frank Darabont. Not that King needed the money (54 books published by 1994 by my count). Originally, Rob Reiner was to direct this film with Harrison Ford as Red and Tom Cruise as Andy, but Darabont decided he would do it for less money. I'm a fan of both Ford and Cruise, but I don't think they can do this film better.Would I recommend it? If you have not seen Shawshank yet, all I can say is watch it before you die. Nobody knows when or how they will die. This is one film you have to watch in whatever time you have remaining.

review: Breaking Free: A Deep Dive into The Shawshank Redemption
main_review:
Hey there, fellow cinephiles and casual movie-goers! Have you ever found yourself pondering the grim realities of life behind bars for a crime you swear on your grandma's grave you didn't commit? Well, put down that stale popcorn and grab a fresh bucket because we're about to plunge headfirst into the labyrinthine walls of Shawshank State Penitentiary. This isn't just any prison; it's a fortress of despair with sky-high walls and even higher stakes. Today, we're dissecting the 1994 cinematic masterpiece known as "The Shawshank Redemption," directed and adapted for the screen by the one and only Frank Darabont. Why, you ask, should you care about a movie that's almost three decades old? Because it's not just another run-of-the-mill prison drama; it's a timeless narrative that delves into the complexities of friendship, the enduring power of hope, and the indomitable resilience of the human spirit. So buckle up, because this is going to be a ride you won't want to miss!The Plot - No Spoilers, I Promise!Imagine it's the 1930s, and you're Andy Dufresne, a banker played by Tim Robbins, who's just been handed a double life sentence for the murder of his wife and her lover. The catch? You're innocent. Welcome to Shawshank, a prison that makes Alcatraz look like a summer camp. From the get-go, the place is a nightmare. On his very first night, Andy witnesses the guards' brutality as they beat an inmate to death. It's a harsh wake-up call to the realities of prison life. But Andy is a survivor. He keeps his head down, mouth shut, and ears open. One day, he overhears a guard complaining about taxes. Seizing the opportunity, Andy offers his financial expertise, and just like that, he becomes the unofficial financial advisor to the guards and eventually even the corrupt Warden Norton. But here's where the plot thickens: a new inmate arrives, someone who could potentially exonerate Andy. But will Warden Norton let that happen? Not if his greed has anything to do with it.The Characters - More Layers Than an Onion
Andy Dufresne: "The Banker Behind Bars"
At first glance, Andy Dufresne seems like a fish out of water-a quiet, almost timid individual who you'd think would never survive a day in Shawshank. But as the story unfolds, we see layers of his character peel away to reveal a man of incredible resilience, intelligence, and hope. His transformation from a meek newcomer to the prison's financial guru is not just a testament to his ingenuity but also an inspiring narrative of human potential.Red: "The Narrator Who Knows How to Get Things"
Morgan Freeman's portrayal of Red is nothing short of iconic. He's the narrator, the philosopher, and the moral compass of the story. His friendship with Andy offers a heartwarming contrast to the bleakness of Shawshank. Through his eyes, we get a panoramic view of life behind bars-from the mundane to the miraculous. His narration isn't just a storytelling device; it's the soul of the movie, offering profound insights into the human condition.Warden Norton: "The Wolf in Sheep's Clothing"
Warden Norton is the epitome of hypocrisy-a man who hides his corrupt and malevolent nature behind a veneer of Christian piety. He quotes the Bible, but his actions are far from Christ-like. He's a master manipulator who knows how to play the system to his advantage. His character serves as a stark reminder that sometimes the real criminals are the ones running the show.The Guards: "The Real Criminals?"
Speaking of running the show, let's talk about the guards. These guys are the foot soldiers of Warden Norton's corrupt regime. Their brutality is not just physical but psychological, serving as a constant reminder to the inmates that they're at the bottom of the food chain. But as Andy rises in prominence, we see subtle shifts in their behavior, adding layers of complexity to their characters.The Director & Screenplay - Frank Darabont's Masterpiece
Frank Darabont took Stephen King's novella and transformed it into a screenplay that's a masterclass in storytelling. The pacing is impeccable, the dialogue is crisp, and the character development is so well-executed that you forget you're watching a movie; you're living it. As film critic Roger Ebert eloquently put it, "The film is an allegory about holding onto a sense of personal worth, despite everything." Darabont crafts a narrative that transcends the confines of its prison setting to explore universal themes of humanity, making you question your own moral compass along the way.Cinematography & Music - A Symphony of Shots
The film's cinematography and music are characters in their own right. The camera work captures the stark contrast between the oppressive walls of Shawshank and the liberating vastness of the outside world. The score by Thomas Newman is a symphony that perfectly complements the highs and lows of the narrative. Peter Travers of Rolling Stone summed it up best when he said, "It's Darabont's accomplished storytelling that makes Shawshank compelling." The visual and auditory elements of the film work in harmony to create an immersive experience that stays with you long after the credits roll.Themes - Not Just a Prison Break
Friendship: "The Bromance That Survived Shawshank"
The friendship between Andy and Red serves as the emotional core of the movie. It's not just a bromance; it's a deep, platonic love story that transcends the grim realities of prison life. Their friendship offers a glimmer of hope and humanity in a world that often seems devoid of both.Hope: "The Thing With Feathers That Perches in the Soul"
Hope is a recurring motif in the film. It's what drives Andy to seek a better life, even within the confines of Shawshank. It's what keeps Red going, despite decades of imprisonment. Hope is the light at the end of a very long, very dark tunnel, and it's what makes the story universally relatable.Justice: "The Long Road to Redemption"
The film raises poignant questions about justice and redemption. Is the legal system truly just? Can one find redemption in a place designed to strip you of your humanity? These themes resonate on a deep, existential level, making the film much more than a simple prison drama.The Impact - Why It's Still Relevant
Despite being nearly three decades old, "The Shawshank Redemption" has left an indelible mark on pop culture. It continues to top IMDb rankings and is frequently cited in discussions about the greatest films of all time. Its themes of friendship, hope, and justice make it a timeless classic that resonates with audiences of all ages.Conclusion
If you've made it this far and still haven't seen "The Shawshank Redemption," then I have to ask: what on Earth are you waiting for? An engraved invitation from Warden Norton himself? This isn't just a movie; it's a transformative experience that challenges your perceptions, tugs at your heartstrings, and leaves you pondering long after the credits have rolled. It's a cinematic journey that you owe it to yourself to take.

There's an essential part of the premise of this movie: you're not supposed to think Andy killed his wife. Andy's a good guy, it clearly was a terrible coincidence.The movie takes great pains to give the impression that there even is a plausible second possible person who would have killed Andy's wife.Here's the thing though. If you were on that jury, you definitely would have voted guilty for Andy. Because there is no way, if you were in that court room, you would be dead certain Andy did it.The beauty of a good movie is the power it has in rewatching, but I think what's rewarding about returning to The Shawshank redemption is thinking about it from the perspective social perspectives. The first time, you're listening to Morgan Freeman tell you about his friend. The second time, you know Andy like he's a friend of your own.But if you watch it again, given the film is in some sense about how we construct and constitute justice, you can consider it from different perspectives.What I think is fascinating about this film, is at some point you realize--despite what the film invites you to believe, Andy absolutely killed his wife. That's not a spoiler--but that's the conclusion I reached after my fourth or fifth time watching the movie. And the beauty of the film is that it only becomes more beautiful and more poignant once you realize that what is one of the most important central conceits for the first time watching the movie is in fact completely implausible, and that the desire to believe Andy didn't kill his wife warps the entire narrative that follows. That's what makes this movie a timeless classic, that at different point in your life you can believe fundamentally different--diametrically opposed--principles of the core tenets of the film. That's craftsmanship.

The Shawshank Redemption is written and directed by Frank Darabont. It is an adaptation of the Stephen King novella Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption. Starring Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman, the film portrays the story of Andy Dufresne (Robbins), a banker who is sentenced to two life sentences at Shawshank State Prison for apparently murdering his wife and her lover. Andy finds it tough going but finds solace in the friendship he forms with fellow inmate Ellis "Red" Redding (Freeman). While things start to pick up when the warden finds Andy a prison job more befitting his talents as a banker. However, the arrival of another inmate is going to vastly change things for all of them.There was no fanfare or bunting put out for the release of the film back in 94, with a title that didn't give much inkling to anyone about what it was about, and with Columbia Pictures unsure how to market it, Shawshank Redemption barely registered at the box office. However, come Academy Award time the film received several nominations, and although it won none, it stirred up interest in the film for its home entertainment release. The rest, as they say, is history. For the film finally found an audience that saw the film propelled to almost mythical proportions as an endearing modern day classic. Something that has delighted its fans, whilst simultaneously baffling its detractors. One thing is for sure, though, is that which ever side of the Shawshank fence you sit on, the film continues to gather new fans and simply will never go away or loose that mythical status.It's possibly the simplicity of it all that sends some haters of the film into cinematic spasms. The implausible plot and an apparent sentimental edge that makes a nonsense of prison life, are but two chief complaints from those that dislike the film with a passion. Yet when characters are this richly drawn, and so movingly performed, it strikes me as churlish to do down a human drama that's dealing in hope, friendship and faith. The sentimental aspect is indeed there, but that acts as a counterpoint to the suffering, degradation and shattering of the soul involving our protagonist. Cosy prison life you say? No chance. The need for human connection is never more needed than during incarceration, surely? And given the quite terrific performances of Robbins (never better) & Freeman (sublimely making it easy), it's the easiest thing in the world to warm to Andy and Red.Those in support aren't faring too bad either. Bob Gunton is coiled spring smarm as Warden Norton, James Whitmore is heart achingly great as the "Birdman Of Shawshank," Clancy Brown is menacing as antagonist Capt. Byron Hadley, William Sadler amusing as Heywood & Mark Rolston is impressively vile as Bogs Diamond. Then there's Roger Deakins' lush cinematography as the camera gracefully glides in and out of the prison offering almost ethereal hope to our characters (yes, they are ours). The music pings in conjunction with the emotional flow of the movie too. Thomas Newman's score is mostly piano based, dovetailing neatly with Andy's state of mind, while the excellently selected soundtrack ranges from the likes of Hank Williams to the gorgeous Le Nozze di Figaro by Mozart....

review: "The Shawshank Redemption" is a beautiful cinematic experience about man's struggle for hope and freedom, and a lot of this thanks to the excellence he carries in his humanity
main_review: There are a select group of films that have achieved the feat of being received with unanimous enthusiasm by both critics and audiences and still having survived the unforgivable test of time virtually intact. This is exactly the case of The Shawshank Redemption, one of the most celebrated films of 1994 and which has already established itself as a classic widely present in the popular imagination. The film directed by Frank Darabont (a feature debutant at the time) reached the position it occupies precisely because it perfectly executes the formula of the redemption drama.Darabont captures the spirit of the works like few others, bringing to the big screen not a transposition identical to the original material, but a reading that matches the source of inspiration. This ability can be seen in "The Mist", "The Green Mile" and "The Shawshank Redemption", films that show how the master of horror also has a talent for dramatic stories. In the production in question, the drama emerges from a man's struggle against the physical and symbolic prisons that arise around him and within him.In the book, successful banker Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) is wrongfully convicted of the murder of his wife and her lover and taken to Shawshank Penitentiary in Maine. His pity: life imprisonment in a place that is a prisoner's nightmare. The routine is terrible because of the cruelty of the director and the guards, but it can also offer friendship with Red (Morgan Freeman), an inmate who leads one of the prison's groups and clandestinely arranges objects requested by colleagues.The evils of incarceration are quickly identified as obstacles to the full freedom of Andy and the others. Isolation from society, severe punishments represented by long sentences or life imprisonment and the confinement guaranteed by walls, fences and guards are enough to express the adversity of prisoners. However, the film goes further and also exposes the authoritarianism of director Warden (Bob Gunton), when he presents to new inmates as an administrator attached to discipline and his own understanding of the Bible, and the truculence of guard Hadley (Clancy Brown), when he beats up a newcomer for crying at night in his cell. Characters and spectators not only feel intimidated, but also feel the threat of Shawshank in the aerial shots of the courtyard and in the magnifying counter-plongée of the place during the protagonist's arrival.In addition to authority figures, the penitentiary's residents themselves also pose some sort of threat. The habit of older prisoners to provoke the new ones increases the situation of tension that already exists, as can be seen in the sequence in which they bet on who would be the first to give in to the pressures of the first night. In the same vein, the tradition of forming different groups that protect their members and intimidate or attack other detainees is another practice carried out by convicts that destabilize the confinement. Anyone who doesn't fit into one of the groups eventually runs into serious problems - that's what happens to Andy, initially a loner raped by the homosexual group, until he approaches Red and becomes part of his group.Shawshank still affects those serving their time in an unconscious, intimate dimension. A long period of imprisonment makes men experience and naturalize a routine that gives some regularity, some certainty to their lives (even if it is bad and adverse): they spend a lot of time in their cells, sunbathe, interact with other prisoners, they eat in the dining halls and face the authorities of the place. Being incarcerated for a long time and consolidating this routine as a habit creates what Red calls an "institutionalized" prisoner, that is, someone who would not survive outside prison because he could not adapt to an environment of freedom. Brooks and Red synthesize the feelings of an ex-convict who regains his freedom, but no longer recognizes the outside world or knows how to act in it - hence, an emptiness that makes them prefer the familiarity that prison awakens.The portrayal of the daily lives of the condemned is carried out in a very coherent way. Darabont seeks simplicity. As in the best films of Clint Eastwood's career, the director of A Dream Freed chooses an almost invisible direction: all his artistic choices privilege the narrative. In addition, he is not afraid to abuse the feature that in writers' jargon is known as "hook". Almost all the elements of the film (Andy's profession, the setting, the objects, small phrases, the secondary characters, etc.) are taken up and reused, with minor changes, for an intensification of the effects. One of the criticisms of using so many hooks is that they make the narrative too obvious, diminishing its originality and complexity. However, what some see as obvious (due to the excess of the same resource) can, on the other hand, be seen as a strong factor of coherence. In my view, Darabont knew how to propose and explore patterns in a way that allowed him to extract the maximum amount of meaning they could offer.The Shawshank Redemption shows the value of freedom, of finding your place in the world, and of real friendship. These are concepts very well worked out by Frank Darabont in his script, put to the test in emotional performances. Even if, at times, the film lacks the narration, much of the relationship between those men in prison is built on silence. The protagonist may be the best example of this, as he is not a talkative person. He tries to stay sane in an unknown world. And, at first, stillness and discretion are his greatest allies. Tim Robbins brings Andy Dufresne to life as a strong-willed person who uses his wits to get what he wants. As much as he is friends with fellow prisoners, he does not allow anyone to know the full extent of his goals. He thinks of the common good, but he has an agenda of his own to fulfill. Morgan Freeman, in turn, makes Red a pleasant-spoken guy who is very sure of his certainties, won over by Andy's temperament and personality. The actors do not hide that there is a love story there, although made by two heterosexual men. This feeling helps both to resist unfavorable situations, such as the constant refusal of parole or the increasing periods of solitary confinement that Andy goes through when defying his superiors.Frank Darabont builds a believable universe, in which "everyone is innocent". Prisoners see their situation through reality and, for them, no one is guilty of the crimes for which they were convicted. The ethics and coexistence of those men is exciting and shows that humanity can exist even among people confined in a prison, deprived of the most valuable right that is freedom. No wonder, the film's most detestable villains are not behind bars, but running the situation, as is the case of director Norton and jailer Byron Hadley (Clancy Brown). We are, after all, seeing the story through the eyes of Red, the narrator of the plot.The most interesting thing about Frank Darabont's work is to note that it examines several ways out of the extreme reality in which its prisoners live, physically, emotionally and even sexually abused by the guards and the inhuman and despotic director. There is resignation, experienced in an automated way by Freeman's character and which he himself will understand as an unfeasible path in a long dialogue with his best friend after Brooks' death. There is the capitulation and denial of life as action and freedom, which Whitmore's character represents by not being able to survive after getting out of prison. Curious that he calls the prison his "home", recognizing himself no longer as a man, but only as a prisoner dependent on his nutshell. Is this not the deepest stage of Sartrean bad faith? A Freedom Dream puts its finger on the wound without mercy - suffering can become the most powerful comfort zone as it denies man himself as responsible for his history. The third outlet for man immersed in such a thorny reality is hope. Put that way, it might sound silly. But the narrative rhythm of the film, with its direction and script that do not hasten the protagonist's evolution, allows us to understand how laborious it is to preserve it in the face of an existence that lashes us not once or twice, but hundreds of times.The film's most iconic still, in which Andy is captured in one of the most recognizable plongée in film history, celebrates the victory of hope in a world that seems to hold none. The character does not earn his freedom in a heroic or glorious way. He reaches it by dragging himself over filth and degradation. This scene throws the lime shovel, once and for all, on the possibility that this was yet another great movie, losing itself in an ending with an easy appeal. A closer look should also understand that here the process also matters a lot. The Shawshank Redemption offers us some tools to face existence. Noble feelings such as friendship and faculties as valuable as human intelligence and creativity, with which Andy moves his companions out of their comfort zones and promotes improvements in his prison life, seem to work as powerful stratagems to preserve the expectation of redemption.Never sounding appealing, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a beautiful cinematic experience about man's struggle for hope and freedom, even amidst the injustices and oppression of the prison system. As powerful as it is, the film doesn't need to use fantastic elements, in the supernatural sense, to be called fantastic. He is like that thanks to the excellence he carries in his humanity.

review: My favorite movie of all time.
main_review: "The Shawshank Redemption," based on the novel by Stephen King, was masterfully directed by Frank Darabont. Adapting a book to the big screen is no easy feat, especially when the source material is as beloved as this one. However, Darabont's work not only stays true to the book, but also stands on its own as a brilliant film. One of the standout performances in the movie is Morgan Freeman's portrayal of Red, which adds a new and powerful dimension to the character. Red's friendship with the protagonist, Andy Dufresne (played by Tim Robbins), adds depth and complexity to the story. Andy's journey is captivating and keeps the viewer engaged throughout the entire film. The fact that Andy is a flawed and complex protagonist only adds to the compelling nature of the story. Additionally, the lack of two-dimensional villains, aside from The Sisters, gives the audience more reasons to root for Andy. I also want to give a special mention to Brooks, whose character arc is heart-wrenching and adds to the emotional impact of the film. Overall, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a must-see movie that offers hope and teaches us to never give up on our dreams.

Twenty-six years after its release, The Shawshank Redemption maintains its top position in the IMDb's rating of top 1000 movies of all time. This fact alone makes the film unquestionably unmissable and worth paying for watching; however, there is more to it than that. A banker Andy Dufrense is wrongfully given a double life sentence for killing his wife and her lover. In the following 19 years of his life, Andy experiences the hardships of prison life and develops a mesmerizing friendship with another inmate, Red. Unlike many movies relying on spectacle and action, The Shawshank Redemption provides emotionally charged conversations and a well-developed look at humanistic emotion. Based on King's novella Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption and directed by Frank Darabont, this drama is neither experimental nor bold, but the smooth plot flow continues to bring the audience odd satisfaction upon watching.

main_review: I'm not going to tell you anything you probably don't already know. Shawshank Redemption is one of the most critically acclaimed movies of all time - for a reason. It all comes together.First off, the story is a tried and true classic, an innocent man accused and wrongly convicted, sentenced to spend the rest of his life in a place he doesn't belong, amongst men who make it all the worse for him because they do belong there. Without hope of release, he overcomes the depression and hopelessness he finds himself in, and decides to seek and find new meaning. Then, in the pursuit of this new revelation, he sees hope again.The details in the writing are outstanding. Stephen King and Frank Darabont have brought the characters to life in their attention to the particular attributes of each of them. Some of the writing reminds me of the way a talented mystery writer formulates a story, allowing for the details to be picked up on by the reader (watcher in this case) if one is looking for them or paying close enough attention.The acting is at the level that should be used for teaching. If you're trying to get into acting, these are actors you can learn something from. Morgan Freeman is well known as an amazing actor, and both before and after this role, he has done impressive work. Tim Robbins is fantastic in this role, and I personally feel he's underutilized in film today. Some of the other roles he's had haven't really made use of his acting chops the way Shawshank did. There are several other actors in the film who do absolutely outstanding work; Bob Gunton, William Sadler, and Clancy Brown rise to the top of my list.The cinematography is great. They do a remarkable job of making you feel the prison environment, enclosed and cramped all the time, except when it fits to do something else.The score really comes in as another character. Each piece is perfectly fit to each scene. I'm imagining seeing the movie without the music and it would still be worthwhile, but it would feel like there's something missing.I've done my best to leave out spoilers because I've been trying to write this for someone who has never seen it. If you haven't, I highly recommend it. It tells an amazing story of the human spirit and the struggle to survive against overwhelming odds, including the reality of what can happen on both sides of the struggle.

Amazing movie, the magic of cinema.The director, Frank Darabont, paints the prison in drab grays and shadows, so that when key events do occur, they seem to have a life of their own.Andy, as played by Robbins, keeps his thoughts to himself. Red, as Freeman plays him, is therefore a crucial element in the story: His close observation of this man, down through the years, provides the way we monitor changes and track the measure of his influence on those around him. And all the time there is something else happening, hidden and secret, which is revealed only at the end."The Shawshank Redemption" is not a depressing story, although I may have made it sound that way. There is a lot of life and humor in it, and warmth in the friendship that builds up between Andy and Red. There is even excitement and suspense, although not when we expect it. But mostly the film is an allegory about holding onto a sense of personal worth, despite everything. If the film is perhaps a little slow in its middle passages, maybe that is part of the idea, too, to give us a sense of the leaden passage of time, before the glory of the final redemption.

review: A little lengthy but still very enjoyable
main_review: Despite it's lengthy runtime, the film is still able to sustain itself all the way through and will keep you fully engaged with it's joyful, hopeful and sometimes even terrifying story the whole time.

Those in support aren't faring too bad either. Bob Gunton is coiled spring smarm as Warden Norton, James Whitmore is heart achingly great as the "Birdman Of Shawshank," Clancy Brown is menacing as antagonist Capt. Byron Hadley, William Sadler amusing as Heywood & Mark Rolston is impressively vile as Bogs Diamond. Then there's Roger Deakins' lush cinematography as the camera gracefully glides in and out of the prison offering almost ethereal hope to our characters (yes, they are ours). The music pings in conjunction with the emotional flow of the movie too. Thomas Newman's score is mostly piano based, dovetailing neatly with Andy's state of mind, while the excellently selected soundtrack ranges from the likes of Hank Williams to the gorgeous Le Nozze di Figaro by Mozart.

review: There's so much to like about this film.
main_review:
The Shawshank Redemption (1994) is a movie I recently rewatched for the first time in a long time on Netflix. The storyline follows a man in prison whose job is to get hard to get things for the prisoners in prison for trade. One day a unique prisoner comes in who is very calculated and has his own ways of getting what he wants. The two men become friends to get through their days serving their life sentences.This movie is directed by Frank Darabont (The Green Mile) and stars
Morgan Freeman (Se7en), Tim Robbins (Mystic River), William Sadler (Demon Knight), Bob Gunton (Daredevil), Clancy Brown (Starship Troopers) and Jeffrey DeMunn (The Mist).The storyline for this picture is absolutely amazing and does a fantastic job of covering so many topics - life in prison, the personalities of those in prison, the struggles of getting out of prison and returning to normalcy and the will to survive. The dialogue is very good and the movie concludes perfectly. There's so much to like about this film. I would score this an easy 10/10 and strongly recommend it.

review: Great Story and Concept, Excellent Acting
main_review: This is a movie that I remember watching before realizing it was based on a Stephen King novella. Part of the reason I saw it was this movie was always on. It is an easy one to jump into at any point and is just good. Jaime and I watched with along with her dad as a movie to end the night as all of us enjoy it. It also was on the Internet Movie Database poster we're working through. I also got the 4K for Christmas and wanted to watch that as well.What we get here is a heartbreaking tale that has good social commentary. We follow Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) as he comes to stay at Shawshank prison. He claims to be innocent but was convicted of murdering his wife. It is there he befriends Ellis Boyd 'Red' Redding (Morgan Freeman) along with his friends. We get to see how these people navigate the prison system and the guards to get better treatment as well as to survive.The commentary I'm referring to is corruption. We have Warden Norton (Bob Gunton) who uses Andy to launder money. There is Captain Hadley (Clancy Brown) who is an enforcer with a short temper. We get to see men raping other men through Bogs Diamond (Mark Rolston) and his crew known as the sisters. There are also the dangers of institutionalization through Brooks Hatlen (James Whitmore) and Red. I don't want the idea of commentary to steer you away if you haven't seen this. We get to see all this in a subtle way that I give credit to writer/director Frank Darabont.I can see why this is number one as one of the greatest movies of all time. We have a great cast of stars and character actors. They all bring their characters to life. This movie feels like the different eras of seeing these prisoners who are in for a long time. The cinematography is also great. I love the subtle effects when prisoners are beaten and seeing how those in power abuse that as well. The soundtrack is also well done on top of that.This is an excellent movie. It is long, but it doesn't feel like it. I highly recommend seeing this one.My Rating: 9 out of 10.

I didn't intend to see this movie at all: I do not like prison movies and I don't normally watch them. I work at a branch library and one day as I was checking The Shawshank Redemption out to one of our older patrons, she said to me, "Whenever I feel down or depressed, I check out this movie and watch it and it always makes me feel better." At the time, I thought that was very strange. One day there was nothing on TV except things I absolutely would not watch under any circumstance or things that I had seen too many times already. I remembered what she said, so I watched it. I have watched it many many times since then and it gets better with every showing.No action, no special effects - just men in prison uniforms talking to each other.The Shawshank Redemption and To Kill a Mockingbird are the best movies I have ever seen. I do not judge it by it's technical merits - I don't really care about that. I have read that Citizen Kane or The Godfather or this or that movie is the best movie ever made. They may have the best technique or be the most influential motion pictures ever made, but not the best. The best movies are ones that touch the soul. It takes a movie like The Shawshank Redemption to touch the sou.
